headline: US asks China to share alerts when AI goes wrong
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met China's vice premier in New York on Sunday and proposed a notification system: each side tells the other when an AI incident could touch national security. Trump and Xi meet in Washington this week. Bessent's case: the number one and number two AI powers should be less opaque with each other.

cover_question.q: What if a computer messes up?

cover_answer: Then you tell the other side. That's the whole idea.
table_question: Would you tell your rival when your project breaks?

5-7.script: America and China both build very smart computer programs called AI. On Sunday, America said: if one of ours does something dangerous, we'll tell you, and you tell us. It's like two neighbors agreeing to shout if either one's grill catches fire. It's only a plan so far, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Two neighbors and a grill fire is a picture. A notification mechanism is not. At this age one vivid detail stands in for the whole story, so the detail is the shout, not the summit.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script trades the notification mechanism for two neighbors who agree to shout about a fire, which is what Bessent described. Expect “is our computer going to be bad?” Nobody has named one that is. This is the grown-ups agreeing to tell each other.

8-12.script: The US and China are racing to build the smartest AI, and neither can see what the other is building. On Sunday the US proposed a fix: if an AI incident on one side could threaten national security, that side tells the other. The buddy check at the pool: you swim your own race, but you look over.
8-12.why: A chain with a rival in it, and a buddy check from the pool. This age is testing whether a rule binds both sides, and this one only works if it does.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether a rule gets applied both ways, and this deal is a rule that only works if both sides keep it. The buddy check is the mechanism: you race, and you still look over. Expect “what if China lies?” Then it doesn't work. Nobody has signed anything; it was discussed on Sunday.

13-17.script: If the US and China are racing to win at AI, why would either tell the other when its AI misfires? Bessent's answer on Sunday: the top two AI powers should be less opaque, so the US proposed an alert system for incidents that touch national security. Can you race someone and share crash reports?
13-17.why: Two true things: a race and a promise to report crashes. A teenager can hold both and argue which one gives.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, and the script hands them the pair: a race to win at AI, which Trump says is the only thing that counts, and a promise to tell the rival when American AI goes wrong. The last question is real. Expect “would China actually tell us?” Say you don't know. Nobody does yet.

5-7.q: What if a computer messes up?
5-7.a: Then the grown-ups in charge tell the other country, and they tell us. That's the new plan.

8-12.q: Why would you tell your rival your AI broke?
8-12.a: Bessent says the top two AI powers should be less opaque.

8-12.q: Has an AI actually done something dangerous?
8-12.a: The articles don't name one. Researchers have warned of risks.

13-17.a: Nobody knows. China's state news called the talks constructive.
Trump and Xi meet this week, and the AI risk warnings are loud.
